sections.heading: Before you start: what is a program?
sections.text:
A Java program is a list of instructions the computer follows from top to bottom, one at a time. Almost every instruction needs to remember something: a score, a name, a patient's heart rate. Remembering is the job of variables.

Every Java instruction is called a statement, and almost every statement ends with a semicolon ;. Think of the semicolon as the full stop of a sentence. Forget it and the compiler (the program that checks your code) will refuse to run it.

sections.heading: What is a variable?
sections.text:
A variable is a named box in the computer's memory. The box has three properties:
1. A type: what kind of thing it can hold (whole number, text, true/false).
2. A name: how you refer to it later.
3. A value: what is inside right now.

In Java the type is decided when you create the box and can never change. A box made for whole numbers will never hold text. This is called static typing and it is why Java catches many mistakes before your program even runs.

sections.heading: Declaring a variable
sections.text:
Declaring means creating the box. The pattern is:
type name = value;

Read it right to left: put the value into the box called name, and the box holds the given type. The single = here is the assignment operator. It does NOT mean "equals" like in maths. It means "store the right side into the left side".

sections.heading: Declare and assign separately
sections.text: You can create the box first and fill it later. Until it has a value, Java will not let you read it (the compiler says variable might not have been initialized).
sections.code:
int score;          // box created, empty
score = 90;         // now it holds 90

int level;
System.out.println(level);  // ERROR: not initialized

sections.heading: Changing a value (reassignment)
sections.text: After the first assignment you may put a new value in the same box. You do NOT repeat the type, because the box already exists. Writing the type again would try to create a second box with the same name, which is an error.
sections.code:
int lives = 3;
lives = 2;          // OK: reassign
lives = lives - 1;  // OK: uses old value (2), stores 1
int lives = 5;      // ERROR: lives already declared

sections.heading: Reading a line of code slowly
sections.text:
Take int lives = lives - 1; style lines in two steps:
Step 1: Java works out the RIGHT side first (uses the current value).
Step 2: it stores the result in the LEFT side.

So lives = lives - 1; when lives is 2 calculates 2 - 1 = 1, then stores 1. The old value is gone.

sections.heading: The common types
sections.text:
int: whole numbers like 7, -40, 0. Range is about -2.1 billion to +2.1 billion.
double: numbers with decimals like 3.14 or -0.5.
boolean: only true or false (lowercase).
char: exactly one character in single quotes, like 'A' or '7'.
String: text in double quotes, like "Hello". It starts with a capital S because it is a class, not a primitive type.

Level 2 covers these in depth. For now, match the value to the type.

sections.heading: Quotes matter
sections.text: Single quotes are for exactly one character. Double quotes are for text of any length. Mixing them is a very common beginner error.
sections.code:
char a = 'A';        // OK
char b = "A";        // ERROR: double quotes make a String
String c = 'Hello';  // ERROR: single quotes are for one char
String d = "Hello";  // OK

sections.heading: Naming rules (the compiler enforces these)
sections.text:
1. Letters, digits, underscore _ and dollar $ only. No spaces, no hyphens.
2. Cannot start with a digit.
3. Cannot be a reserved keyword (class, int, if, for, return, true...).
4. Case-sensitive: score, Score and SCORE are three different variables.
sections.code:
int heart-rate = 70;   // ERROR: hyphen
int 2fast = 1;         // ERROR: starts with digit
int class = 3;         // ERROR: keyword
int my score = 5;      // ERROR: space
int heartRate = 70;    // OK

sections.heading: Naming conventions (good habits)
sections.text:
These are not enforced, but every Java programmer follows them:
camelCase for variables and methods: first word lowercase, each next word capitalized (patientStatus).
PascalCase for classes: every word capitalized (CoderHero).
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants (MAX_LIVES).
Pick names that explain themselves: heartRate is far better than x.

sections.heading: Constants with final
sections.text: Put final in front and the value is locked after the first assignment. Use it for values that should never change, like a maximum or a tax rate. Trying to change it is a compile error, which protects you from accidental bugs.
sections.code:
final int MAX_LIVES = 3;
MAX_LIVES = 5;   // ERROR: cannot assign a value to final variable

sections.heading: Declare several at once
sections.text: Variables of the same type can share one declaration, separated by commas. Each can have its own value or none.
sections.code:
int a = 1, b = 2, c;
c = a + b;   // 3

sections.heading: Showing a value on screen
sections.text: To see what a variable holds, print it. System.out.println(...) prints and moves to a new line. System.out.print(...) prints without a new line. Text goes in double quotes; a variable name is written without quotes.
sections.code:
int age = 17;
System.out.println(age);        // prints 17
System.out.println("age");      // prints the word age
System.out.println("Age: " + age);  // prints Age: 17

sections.heading: Worked example: trace the values
sections.text: Follow each line and track the boxes. This habit of tracing is the best way to understand code.
sections.code:
int a = 5;        // a = 5
int b = 10;       // a = 5,  b = 10
int temp = a;     // a = 5,  b = 10, temp = 5
a = b;            // a = 10, b = 10, temp = 5
b = temp;         // a = 10, b = 5,  temp = 5
// a and b have been swapped!

sections.heading: Typical compiler errors and what they mean
sections.text:
';' expected: you forgot a semicolon (look at the line above the one reported).
cannot find symbol: you used a name that was never declared, or you misspelled it, or the capitalization differs.
incompatible types: the value does not fit the type, like putting "Hi" into an int.
variable already defined: you declared the same name twice.
might not have been initialized: you read a variable that has no value yet.

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. Which line is wrong? (a) int x = 4; (b) String s = 'hi'; (c) double d = 2.5;
Q2. After int n = 3; n = n + 4; what does n hold?
Q3. Is Score the same variable as score?

Answers: Q1: (b), single quotes are for one char, so use "hi". Q2: 7. Q3: No, Java is case-sensitive.

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Variables
sections.text:
Declare: type name;
Assign: name = value;
Both: type name = value;
Constant: final type NAME = value;
Statements end with ;
Strings: "double"   chars: 'single'
Names: camelCase, no spaces, no leading digit, not a keyword, case-sensitive
Print: System.out.println(x);
Top mistakes: missing ;, wrong quotes, using a variable before declaring or assigning it, declaring the same name twice.

sections.heading: Why types matter
sections.text: Computers store everything as bits, so Java needs to know how to interpret them. The type tells Java how much memory to use and which operations make sense. You can add two numbers, but multiplying two true/false values makes no sense, and Java will tell you so.

sections.heading: The whole-number types
sections.text:
byte (-128 to 127), short (about +/-32 thousand), int (about +/-2.1 billion), long (about +/-9 quintillion).
In practice use int by default and long when numbers get huge. A long literal needs an L at the end.

sections.heading: The decimal types
sections.text: double is the default for decimals (about 15 digits of precision). float is smaller and less precise; a float literal needs an f. Use double unless you have a reason not to.

sections.heading: Decimals are approximate
sections.text: Computers store decimals in binary, so some values cannot be stored exactly. Never compare doubles with == after calculating. Money is usually stored as whole cents in an int, or with the BigDecimal class.

sections.heading: boolean and char
sections.text:
boolean holds true or false and powers every decision in your program.
char holds one character. Under the hood it is a number (its Unicode code), so 'A' is 65 and 'a' is 97. That is why you can do maths with chars.

sections.heading: Arithmetic operators
sections.text: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide, % remainder (modulus). % gives what is left over after dividing, which is surprisingly useful.

sections.heading: Uses of the % operator
sections.text:
Even or odd: n % 2 == 0 means even.
Divisible by k: n % k == 0.
Wrap around: index % length keeps an index inside a range.
Last digit: n % 10.
Clock maths: (hour + 5) % 12.

sections.heading: Integer division
sections.text: When both operands are ints, Java does whole-number division and throws away the decimal part (it truncates, it does not round). To get decimals, make at least one side a double before the division happens.
sections.code:
int a = 7 / 2;           // 3
double b = 7 / 2;        // 3.0  (int division happened first!)
double c = 7 / 2.0;      // 3.5
double d = (double) 7 / 2; // 3.5
int e = -7 / 2;          // -3  (toward zero)

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.text: Same as maths: 1. parentheses, 2. * / % (left to right), 3. + - (left to right). When unsure, add parentheses; they cost nothing and make the code clearer.

sections.heading: Mixing types and casting
sections.text: Widening (small type into a bigger one, like int into double) is automatic and safe. Narrowing (big into small, like double into int) can lose data, so Java forces you to write a cast in parentheses. A cast to int cuts off the decimals; it does not round.
sections.code:
double d = 5;            // OK: 5.0
int i = 9.99;            // ERROR: possible lossy conversion
int j = (int) 9.99;      // 9
int k = (int) 9.99 + 1;  // 10  (cast applies to 9.99 only)
long big = 100;          // OK widening

sections.heading: Shortcut assignment operators
sections.text:
These update a variable using its own value:
x += 5 means x = x + 5
x -= 5 means x = x - 5
x *= 2 means x = x * 2
x /= 2 and x %= 3 work the same way.
sections.code:
int score = 10;
score += 5;    // 15
score *= 2;    // 30
score -= 10;   // 20
score /= 4;    // 5

sections.heading: Increment and decrement
sections.text:
x++ adds 1, x-- subtracts 1. There are two forms:
Post (x++): use the current value, THEN change it.
Pre (++x): change it FIRST, then use the new value.
Alone on a line they behave the same; the difference only shows inside bigger expressions.
sections.code:
int a = 5;
int b = a++;   // b = 5, a = 6
int c = ++a;   // a = 7, c = 7
int d = a--;   // d = 7, a = 6

sections.heading: Comparison operators
sections.text:
Comparisons produce a boolean:
== equal, != not equal, < less, > greater, <= less or equal, >= greater or equal.

The classic bug: = assigns, == compares.
sections.code:
int hp = 50;
boolean low = hp < 20;      // false
boolean full = hp == 100;   // false
boolean alive = hp != 0;    // true

sections.heading: Logical operators
sections.text:
&& (AND): true only if BOTH sides are true.
|| (OR): true if AT LEAST ONE side is true.
! (NOT): flips true to false and back.

Truth table:
true && true = true
true && false = false
false || true = true
false || false = false
!true = false

sections.heading: Short-circuit evaluation
sections.text: Java stops as soon as the answer is known. In a && b, if a is false, b is never evaluated. In a || b, if a is true, b is skipped. This is used for safe checks.
sections.code:
int x = 0;
boolean safe = (x != 0) && (10 / x > 1);  // no crash: right side skipped

sections.heading: Joining text with +
sections.text: With Strings, + means join (concatenate). Evaluation goes left to right, so the order of numbers and strings changes the result.
sections.code:
"Level " + 2       // "Level 2"
1 + 2 + "go"       // "3go"   (1+2 first)
"go" + 1 + 2       // "go12"  (join each)
"go" + (1 + 2)     // "go3"

sections.heading: The Math class
sections.text: Java ships a toolbox of math helpers. Call them with Math. in front.
sections.code:
Math.max(3, 9);       // 9
Math.min(3, 9);       // 3
Math.abs(-7);         // 7
Math.pow(2, 3);       // 8.0
Math.sqrt(16);        // 4.0
Math.round(2.6);      // 3
Math.random();        // 0.0 up to (not including) 1.0

sections.heading: Worked example: trace it
sections.text: What does this print? Work through it before reading the answer.

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. What is 9 / 2 in Java?
Q2. What is 9 % 2?
Q3. What is 1 + 2 + "3" + 4?
Q4. What does int x = (int) 7.9; store?
Q5. What is the result of true || false && false?

Answers: Q1: 4. Q2: 1. Q3: "334" (3 first, then joins). Q4: 7. Q5: true (&& is done before ||).

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Types and operators
sections.text:
Whole: byte, short, int, long(L)   Decimal: double, float(f)
Other: boolean, char, String
Arithmetic: + - * / %
int / int = int, decimals dropped
Cast: (int) x cuts decimals, (double) x widens
Shortcuts: += -= *= /= %= ++ --
Compare: == != < > <= >=
Logic: && || !
Order: () then * / % then + - then comparisons then && then ||
Even test: n % 2 == 0

sections.heading: Programs that decide
sections.text: So far your code ran every line in order. Real programs must choose: if the fuel is low, land; if the password is wrong, show an error. Choosing is done with conditions. A condition is any expression whose result is a boolean (true or false).

sections.heading: The if statement
sections.text:
if (condition) { code }
If the condition is true, the code inside the braces runs. If false, Java skips the whole block and continues after it. The condition MUST be in parentheses and MUST be a boolean.

sections.heading: if / else
sections.text: Add else for the other case. Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both, never neither.

sections.heading: else if chains
sections.text: For more than two outcomes, chain tests. Java checks them from the top down, runs the first block whose condition is true, and skips everything after it. Order matters: put the strictest test first.

sections.heading: Order mistake to avoid
sections.text: If you put the loosest test first, it swallows the others. Here every score above 70 prints C, even 99.

sections.heading: Braces and indentation
sections.text: Braces { } group the statements that belong to the if. Without braces, only the next single statement belongs to it, which causes sneaky bugs. Always use braces, and indent the inside so the structure is visible.

sections.heading: Mistake: = instead of ==
sections.text: = assigns, == compares. Inside an if, writing = with an int is a compile error because an assignment is not a boolean. (With a boolean variable it compiles but silently changes the value, which is even worse.)
sections.code:
if (x = 5) { }          // ERROR: int cannot be converted to boolean
if (x == 5) { }         // correct

sections.heading: Mistake: the stray semicolon
sections.text: A semicolon right after the condition ends the if with an empty body. The braces below then become an ordinary block that always runs.

sections.heading: Comparing Strings
sections.text: == on Strings checks whether two variables point at the same object, not whether the text matches. Always compare text with .equals(), or .equalsIgnoreCase() to ignore capitals.
sections.code:
String name = "Kai";
if (name.equals("Kai")) { }          // correct
if (name.equalsIgnoreCase("KAI")) { }  // true
if (name == "Kai") { }               // unreliable, avoid

sections.heading: Combining conditions
sections.text: Use && (and), || (or), ! (not) to build one condition from several. Never write a chained comparison like 0 < x < 10; Java cannot do that. Write each test separately.
sections.code:
if (age >= 13 && age <= 19) { }       // teenager
if (day.equals("Sat") || day.equals("Sun")) { }
if (!(score < 50)) { }                // same as score >= 50
if (0 < x < 10) { }                   // ERROR

sections.heading: Nested if
sections.text: An if can sit inside another if. The inner test is only reached when the outer one is true. Use it when a second decision depends on the first, but do not nest too deeply; combine with && when you can.

sections.heading: The dangling else
sections.text: An else always belongs to the nearest unmatched if above it, regardless of how you indent. Braces remove all doubt.

sections.heading: The ternary operator
sections.text:
A compact if/else that produces a value:
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
Good for simple choices. For anything longer, use a normal if.
sections.code:
String result = (score >= 75) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
int bigger = (a > b) ? a : b;

sections.heading: The switch statement
sections.text: Use switch when one variable is compared against several fixed values. It works with int, char, String and enums. Each case ends with break; default runs if nothing matches.

sections.heading: Fall-through
sections.text: If you forget break, Java keeps running into the next case, even if it does not match. This is called fall-through. It is usually a bug, but you can use it on purpose to share one result between several cases.

sections.heading: switch with Strings
sections.text: switch can compare Strings (it uses equals internally). The text must match exactly, including capitals.

sections.heading: if or switch?
sections.text:
switch: one value, many exact matches (menus, days, commands).
if / else if: ranges (score >= 90), or tests combining several variables.

sections.heading: Worked example: trace it
sections.text: What prints when x = 15?

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. What is wrong: if (score = 100) ?
Q2. What does a switch do when a case has no break?
Q3. How do you check that String s equals "go"?
Q4. What prints: int n = 8; if (n % 2 == 0) print("even"); else print("odd");

Answers: Q1: it assigns instead of comparing; use ==. Q2: it falls through into the next case. Q3: s.equals("go"). Q4: even.

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Conditions
sections.text:
if (cond) { } cond must be boolean, in ( )
else if top-down, first true wins
else the leftover case
Always use braces
== for numbers/chars, .equals() for Strings
&& || ! combine; no 0 < x < 10 chains
?: condition ? a : b
switch (value) { case X: ... break; default: ... }
Bugs: = vs ==, ; after if(...), missing break, wrong test order

sections.heading: Why loops exist
sections.text: Imagine printing the numbers 1 to 1000. You do not want to write 1000 lines. A loop repeats a block of code as many times as needed. Java has three loops: for, while and do-while. All three can do the same job; they differ in how they are written and when they check.

sections.heading: The for loop
sections.text:
for (start; test; update) { body }
1. start runs once, at the beginning.
2. test is checked before every round. If true, the body runs. If false, the loop ends.
3. update runs after each round.
Then it goes back to step 2.

sections.heading: Tracing a for loop
sections.text:
Make a table of what happens each round for for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++):
Start: i = 0
Test 0 < 3: true, run body, i becomes 1
Test 1 < 3: true, run body, i becomes 2
Test 2 < 3: true, run body, i becomes 3
Test 3 < 3: false, loop ends.
The body ran 3 times with i = 0, 1, 2. The variable i is only visible inside the loop.

sections.heading: Counting patterns
sections.text: Changing the start, test and update gives every pattern. Watch the boundary: < versus <= changes how many rounds you get.

sections.heading: Off-by-one errors
sections.text: The most common loop bug is running one time too many or too few. Rule: starting at 0 with < n runs exactly n times. Starting at 1 with <= n also runs exactly n times. Mixing start 0 with <= n runs n + 1 times.

sections.heading: The while loop
sections.text:
while (condition) { body }
Checks the condition before every round. If it is false at the very start, the body never runs. Use it when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. Something inside must eventually make the condition false.

sections.heading: The do-while loop
sections.text:
do { body } while (condition);
Runs the body first, then checks. So it always runs at least once. Perfect for menus and input checks ("ask, then check if the answer was valid"). Note the semicolon after the condition.

sections.heading: Which loop should I use?
sections.text:
for: you know the number of rounds (count from a to b).
while: repeat until something happens; may run zero times.
do-while: must run at least once.

sections.heading: Infinite loops
sections.text: A loop whose test never becomes false runs forever and freezes your program. Common causes: forgetting to update the variable, updating in the wrong direction, or a test that is always true.

sections.heading: break and continue
sections.text: break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one (in a for loop, the update still runs).

sections.heading: The accumulator pattern
sections.text: Make a variable before the loop and update it each round. This is the foundation of totals, counts, maximums and averages.

sections.heading: Nested loops
sections.text: A loop inside a loop. For every single round of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely. Outer 3 rounds x inner 2 rounds = 6 total runs of the inner body.

sections.heading: Drawing a triangle
sections.text: Nested loops are great for patterns. Here the inner loop prints as many stars as the current row number, then println moves to the next line.

sections.heading: Mistake: semicolon after the loop header
sections.text: for (...); or while (...); creates an empty loop. The loop spins doing nothing, then the block below runs once.

sections.heading: Worked example: trace it
sections.text: What does this print?

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) run?
Q2. How many times does do { } while (false); run?
Q3. What does continue do?
Q4. What is wrong with while (n > 0) { print(n); } if n starts at 5?

Answers: Q1: 7. Q2: once. Q3: skips to the next round. Q4: n never changes, so it loops forever.

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Loops
sections.text:
for (start; test; update) { }   known count
while (test) { }   test first, may run 0 times
do { } while (test);   runs at least once
break leave the loop, continue skip this round
i < n from 0 = n rounds
Accumulator: total = 0; then total += value;
Nested: inner runs fully per outer round
Bugs: infinite loop, off-by-one, ; after the header

sections.heading: Why arrays?
sections.text: Suppose you store 30 student marks. Making 30 separate variables is painful. An array is one variable that holds many values of the same type, side by side in memory. You reach each value by its position number, called the index.

sections.heading: Creating arrays
sections.text:
Two ways. 1. List the values directly. 2. Create an empty array of a given size with new; the slots get default values (0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects).

The square brackets go after the type: int[] means "array of int".
sections.code:
int[] ids = {101, 102, 103};          // direct values
String[] names = {"Ana", "Ben", "Cy"};
int[] marks = new int[5];             // 0 0 0 0 0
boolean[] flags = new boolean[3];     // false false false

sections.heading: Indexes start at 0
sections.text:
The first item is index 0, not 1. For an array of length 5, the valid indexes are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The last index is always length - 1.

Picture it: ids = {101, 102, 103}
index 0 holds 101
index 1 holds 102
index 2 holds 103

sections.heading: Array length
sections.text: arr.length gives how many items the array holds. For arrays there are no parentheses (it is a field). The size is fixed forever once created.

sections.heading: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
sections.text: If you use an index that does not exist (negative, or length or more), the program crashes at runtime with this exception. It is the classic off-by-one bug.

sections.heading: Looping over an array
sections.text: Arrays and for loops go together. Use i < arr.length as the test. A for-each loop reads each value without an index, but cannot tell you the position.

sections.heading: Common algorithm: total and average
sections.text: Add every element with an accumulator, then divide. Cast to double so the average keeps its decimals.

sections.heading: Common algorithm: find the largest
sections.text: Assume the first item is the largest, then compare each other item and replace when you find a bigger one.

sections.heading: Common algorithm: search
sections.text: Linear search: check each item until you find the target.

sections.heading: Common algorithm: reverse in place
sections.text: Swap the first with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on, stopping at the middle.

sections.heading: Arrays are references
sections.text: An array variable holds a reference (an address), not the data itself. Assigning one array variable to another makes both point at the same array. Changing one changes the other. To make a real copy, use Arrays.copyOf.

sections.heading: Printing and sorting
sections.text: Printing an array directly shows a useless address like [I@1b6d3586. Use the Arrays helper class (import java.util.Arrays).

sections.heading: Two-dimensional arrays
sections.text: An array of arrays, like a table with rows and columns. You use two indexes: grid[row][col]. Use nested loops to walk through it.

sections.heading: Strings: text as objects
sections.text: A String is a sequence of characters, also numbered from 0. Unlike an array, a String is an object with many helpful methods, and its length uses parentheses: s.length(). Strings are immutable: methods never change the original, they return a new String.
sections.code:
String s = "Hello";
s.length();         // 5
s.charAt(0);        // 'H'
s.charAt(4);        // 'o'
s.toUpperCase();    // "HELLO"   (s itself is unchanged)
s = s.toUpperCase(); // now s is "HELLO"

sections.heading: Essential String methods
sections.text:
substring(a, b): from index a up to but NOT including b.
substring(a): from a to the end.
indexOf(x): position of the first match, or -1.
contains(x), startsWith(x), endsWith(x): true/false.
replace(old, new), trim() (removes outer spaces), isEmpty().
sections.code:
String s = "coder hero";
s.substring(0, 5);     // "coder"
s.substring(6);        // "hero"
s.indexOf("hero");     // 6
s.indexOf("z");        // -1
s.contains("der");     // true
s.replace("hero", "cat");  // "coder cat"
"  hi  ".trim();       // "hi"

sections.heading: Comparing Strings
sections.text: Never use == for text. It compares memory addresses, not letters. Use .equals() (exact match), .equalsIgnoreCase(), or .compareTo() (returns 0 if equal, negative if it comes before, positive if after).

sections.heading: Looping through a String
sections.text: Use charAt with a for loop to examine each character. Here is a vowel counter.

sections.heading: split and join
sections.text: split cuts a String into an array of pieces. String.join glues an array back together.

sections.heading: Building text efficiently
sections.text: Because Strings are immutable, joining inside a big loop creates many throwaway objects. Use StringBuilder to build text in place.

sections.text: What does this print?

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. What is the last valid index of an array of length 8?
Q2. What does "Boris".charAt(0) return?
Q3. What does "hello".substring(1, 4) return?
Q4. Why does int[] b = a; not copy the array?
Q5. arr.length or arr.length() for an array?

Answers: Q1: 7. Q2: 'B'. Q3: "ell". Q4: both variables refer to the same array. Q5: arr.length (no parentheses).

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Arrays and Strings
sections.text:
Create: int[] a = {1,2,3}; or new int[5];
Index: a[0] first, a[a.length-1] last
Array size: a.length   String size: s.length()
Crash: index < 0 or >= length
Loop: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
Print array: Arrays.toString(a)   Sort: Arrays.sort(a)
String: charAt, substring(a,b), indexOf, contains, replace, trim, split
Compare text: .equals(), never ==
Strings never change; methods return new Strings
b = a shares the same array

sections.heading: Why methods?
sections.text: A method is a named block of code that does one job. Instead of copying the same ten lines in five places, you write them once and call the method by name. Benefits: less repeated code, easier fixes (change it in one place), and programs you can read like a list of steps.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a method
sections.text:
modifiers returnType name(parameters) { body }
static: lets main call it directly without creating an object.
returnType: the type of value handed back (int, String, boolean...). Use void if nothing comes back.
name: camelCase, usually a verb (calculateTotal, printReport).
parameters: the inputs, each with a type and a name.

sections.heading: Calling a method
sections.text: Write the name followed by the arguments in parentheses, in the same count, order and type as the parameters. Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the actual values you pass in the call.
sections.code:
int total = add(2, 3);        // total = 5
greet("Kai");                 // prints Hello, Kai
System.out.println(add(10, 4) * 2);   // 28

sections.heading: What happens during a call
sections.text:
1. Java evaluates the arguments.
2. It copies them into the parameters.
3. It jumps into the method and runs the body.
4. At return (or the closing brace for void), it jumps back to where the call was, replacing the call with the returned value.

sections.heading: Return values
sections.text: return value; ends the method immediately and sends the value to the caller. A non-void method must return a value of the declared type on every possible path. Code after a return is unreachable, which is a compile error.

sections.heading: void methods
sections.text: A void method does something (prints, changes data) but gives nothing back. You cannot store its result. You can still write a bare return; to leave early.

sections.heading: Parameters are copies (pass by value)
sections.text: For primitives (int, double, boolean, char), Java passes a copy of the value. Changing the parameter inside the method does not change the caller's variable.

sections.heading: Objects and arrays share the original
sections.text: For arrays and objects, the copy that gets passed is a copy of the reference (the address). So the method can change the contents of the original array. But reassigning the parameter to a different array does not affect the caller.

sections.heading: Returning a result instead
sections.text: To get a changed primitive out of a method, return it and store it.

sections.heading: Multiple parameters and order
sections.text: Arguments are matched to parameters strictly by position. Swapping them silently changes the meaning.

sections.heading: Overloading
sections.text: Several methods may share one name if their parameter lists differ (different number or types). Java picks the right one from your arguments. A different return type alone is not enough.

sections.heading: Scope: where variables live
sections.text: A variable exists only inside the braces where it was declared. Variables declared inside a method (and its parameters) are local: no other method can see them, and the same name can be reused safely in different methods. A loop variable like i vanishes after the loop.

sections.heading: The main method
sections.text: Every Java program starts at main. Its header must be exactly this. Other methods only run if main (or something main calls) calls them.

sections.heading: Methods calling methods
sections.text: Methods can call other methods, building big jobs from small ones. Each call gets its own fresh set of local variables.

sections.heading: Recursion (a method calling itself)
sections.text: A recursive method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. It needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (a smaller call). Without a base case you get a StackOverflowError.

sections.heading: Designing good methods
sections.text:
One job each: a method should do one thing and have a name that says it.
Short: if it grows past a screen, split it.
Return, do not print: a method that returns a value is reusable; one that only prints is hard to reuse.
Avoid surprises: do not change inputs unless the name says so.

sections.heading: Worked example: trace it
sections.text: What does this print?

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. What does a void method return?
Q2. If void inc(int n) { n++; } is called with x = 5, what is x after?
Q3. Can two methods in one class both be named print?
Q4. What is wrong with a method int f(int n) { if (n > 0) return 1; } ?

Answers: Q1: nothing. Q2: still 5 (copy). Q3: yes, if their parameters differ (overloading). Q4: no return when n is 0 or less, so a return is missing on one path.

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Methods
sections.text:
Define: static returnType name(type param, ...) { ... }
Call: name(args);
void returns nothing; return x; sends x back and exits
Every path of a non-void method must return
Arguments match parameters in count, order and type
Primitives are passed by copy; arrays/objects share contents
Overload: same name, different parameters
Scope: locals live only in their braces
main: public static void main(String[] args)
Recursion needs a base case

sections.heading: Thinking in objects
sections.text: Real programs model real things: a hero, a patient, a bank account. Object-oriented programming (OOP) bundles a thing's data (what it knows) and its actions (what it can do) into one unit. Java is built around this idea.

sections.heading: Class versus object
sections.text:
A class is a blueprint: it describes what every Hero has and can do. An object (or instance) is one actual Hero built from that blueprint, created with new. One class can produce thousands of objects, each with its own data.

Analogy: the class is the cookie cutter, the objects are the cookies.

sections.heading: Fields and methods
sections.text: Fields (also called attributes or instance variables) are variables that belong to each object. Methods are the actions. You reach both with the dot operator.

sections.heading: Constructors
sections.text: A constructor is special code that runs when you use new, so every object starts in a valid state. Rules: it has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void).

sections.heading: The this keyword
sections.text: this means "the object I am working inside right now". It is how you separate a field from a parameter with the same name: this.name is the field, plain name is the parameter. Without this, name = name would assign the parameter to itself and the field stays empty.

sections.heading: Default constructor
sections.text: If you write no constructor at all, Java supplies an invisible empty one so new Hero() works. The moment you write any constructor, that free one disappears. Then new Hero() fails unless you add one yourself.
sections.code:
Hero() { }                    // add back if you still want new Hero()
Hero h = new Hero();

sections.heading: Overloaded constructors
sections.text: A class can have several constructors with different parameters. One can call another using this(...) as its very first line to avoid repeating code.

sections.heading: Encapsulation: private and public
sections.text:
If every field is open, any code can set power = -999 and break your object. Encapsulation means hiding the data and controlling access.
private: visible only inside the class.
public: visible everywhere.
Provide getters (read) and setters (write, with checks).

sections.heading: Instance versus static
sections.text: Instance members belong to each object (every Hero has its own name). static members belong to the class itself and exist once, shared by all objects. Call static members through the class name. A static method cannot use instance fields directly because there is no particular object.

sections.heading: Object references
sections.text: An object variable does not hold the object; it holds a reference (an address) to it. Copying the variable copies the address, so both variables point at the same object. Changing it through one name changes it for both.

sections.heading: null and NullPointerException
sections.text: null means "this variable points at no object". Calling a method or reading a field on null crashes with NullPointerException. Declared but unassigned object fields start as null. Guard with a check when null is possible.

sections.heading: Inheritance
sections.text: extends makes a new class that automatically has everything its parent (superclass) has, plus its own additions. It models an "is-a" relationship: a Doctor is a Staff member. It avoids duplicating shared code.

sections.heading: super
sections.text: super(...) as the first line of a constructor calls the parent's constructor. super.method() calls the parent's version of a method. If the parent has no no-argument constructor, the child must call super(...) explicitly.

sections.heading: Overriding methods
sections.text: A child class can replace an inherited method with its own version by writing a method with the same name and parameters. Add @Override so the compiler checks you spelled it right.

sections.heading: Polymorphism
sections.text: A parent-type variable can hold any child object. When you call an overridden method, Java runs the child's version at runtime. This lets one loop treat many different kinds of objects the same way.
sections.code:
Villain v = new Corruptor();   // parent type, child object
v.attack();                    // prints Hit then Corrupt!

Villain[] team = { new Villain(), new Corruptor() };
for (Villain x : team) x.attack();   // each does its own version

sections.heading: toString and printing objects
sections.text: Printing an object normally shows something like Hero@1b6d3586. Override toString to control what appears.

sections.heading: equals for objects
sections.text: == on objects asks "are these the exact same object?". If you want "do they hold the same data?", you write an equals method. Strings already do this, which is why .equals() works on them.

sections.heading: Putting it together
sections.text: A small complete class showing a constructor, private data, validation, a method and toString. Study how each piece connects.

sections.heading: Practice: try to answer first
sections.text:
Q1. What is the difference between a class and an object?
Q2. Why does a constructor have no return type?
Q3. What does this refer to?
Q4. What happens if you call a method on a null reference?
Q5. Why make fields private?

Answers: Q1: class = blueprint, object = one instance made with new. Q2: it is not a normal method; it only initializes the new object. Q3: the current object. Q4: NullPointerException. Q5: so outside code cannot put the object into an invalid state; access goes through checked getters/setters.

sections.heading: Cheat sheet: Classes and objects
sections.text:
class = blueprint; object = instance made with new
Field = data; method = action; dot reaches both
Constructor: same name as class, no return type
this = current object; this.x = x;
private fields + public getters/setters = encapsulation
static = one copy shared by the class
extends = inherit; super(...) calls the parent constructor
@Override replaces an inherited method
Reference: b = a shares one object; == compares addresses
null + method call = NullPointerException
toString() controls printing
